t: Sun Yat-sen first set out the Principles of nationalism, democracy and people's welfare in 1905, and the Tongmenghui, formed in Tokyo that year, put them in its manifesto.
Sun's democracy rested on a distinction between the people's sovereignty and the government's ability, a government of five branches and a period of political tutelage before constitutional rule.
After Sun's death in 1925 the Kuomintang made the Principles, as Sun gave them in his 1924 lectures and Chiang Kai-shek interpreted them, the official ideology of its state.
dyk: The name “Three Principles of the People” comes from Feng Ziyou, who later claimed that while editing a Hong Kong Tongmenghui paper he shortened the phrase “promoting nationalism, democracy, and people's welfare” into the term.
ev: Sun Yat-sen founds the radically anti-Qing Revive China Society
Sun first sets out the ideas behind his Principles in a speech in Brussels, and the Tongmenghui is formed in Tokyo
Sun reiterates the idea of a political transition in the Chinese Revolutionary Party, with an indefinite revolutionary period of party rule
Sun dies of liver cancer after signing a testament that urges the Kuomintang to hold fast to the Principles
The Organic Law reorganises the Nationalist government on the principle of political tutelage, with five branches
Sun's Whampoa address, whose opening line invokes the Principles, becomes the Kuomintang's party anthem
Mao Zedong's On New Democracy reads the Principles as the “New Three Principles of the People”
Singapore's People's Power Party is founded with the Principles as its official guiding ideology

f.thinkers: Sun Yat-sen, who set out the Principles; Hu Hanmin, Wang Jingwei and Feng Ziyou, who fleshed them out in Minbao; Zhu Zhixin, who defended the Tongmenghui's “state socialism”; Chiang Kai-shek, who interpreted them as party leader; Dai Jitao, whose conservative reading the Kuomintang followed; Liang Qichao, the reformist rival whose ideas on the nation and the general will left their mark
f.texts: the Tongmenghui manifesto (1905); Sun's article in the first issue of Minbao (1905); The International Development of China; The Fundamentals of National Reconstruction (1924); Sun's lectures, published as The Three Principles of the People (English translation by Frank Price, 1927); Sun's political testament (1925, drafted by Wang Jingwei)
f.ideas: nationalism, with China's revival from imperial domination; democracy, with the four powers of the people (suffrage, recall, initiative, referendum) and a five-branch government; people's livelihood, covering clothing, food, housing and mobility; land equalisation by self-assessment; a distinction between the sovereignty of the people and the ability of the government; political tutelage before constitutional government; the Confucian ideal of Datong
f.today: the Kuomintang made the Principles the official ideology of its state, and after its government's retreat to Taiwan Chiang Kai-shek added texts on education and leisure; the Chinese Communist Party honours Sun, less so the Principles, and in Deng Xiaoping's era linked his economic plans to the Four Modernisations; Singapore's People's Power Party, founded in 2015, took them as its guiding ideology
